tagline: Along US 24, river towns recall the Santa Fe trade.
intro: The US 24 corridor links Lexington, Dover and Waverly in Lafayette County. Lexington occupies the Missouri River bluffs; at Waverly, US 24 and US 65 cross the river together. The Missouri Department of Transportation identifies Show Me Santa Fe Trails on its scenic-byway map.

The older Santa Fe Trail followed portions of the Osage Trace and Medicine Trails across Missouri. After crossing the Missouri near Arrow Rock, it followed roughly the course of present-day US 24 through Lexington toward Fort Osage and Independence. Lexington supplied merchants and outfitters preparing travelers for the western trails.
For an eastward drive, begin at Lexington, continue through Dover and finish at Waverly’s Missouri River crossing. The bridge there opened in 2004, replacing a crossing built in 1922.

moments.title: Lexington
moments.text: Lexington’s outfitting trade joined river commerce to overland journeys. Merchants supplied trappers, traders and emigrants bound for the Santa Fe, California and Oregon trails. Goods sent west from the town were valued at $450,000 in 1843. Hemp, tobacco and cattle helped build the surrounding agricultural economy, and Lexington and Lafayette County held one of Missouri’s largest enslaved populations. The steamboat wharf became a commercial center, supplied with fuel from coal mines in the river bluffs. On Main Street, the Greek Revival courthouse dates to 1847. The town retains more than 150 pre-Civil War homes and public buildings.

moments.title: Dover
moments.text: Dover’s post office preceded its town plan by four years: the postal name was in use in 1835, while the town was platted in 1839. A nearby church supplied the community’s name. Dover remains a small Lafayette County town: the 2020 census counted 83 residents.

moments.title: Waverly
moments.text: The river crossing at Waverly has changed since the previous bridge was built in 1922. That bridge had a deck just 20 feet wide; its replacement opened in August 2004, and the older structure was demolished the following year. US 24 and US 65 share the present crossing over the Missouri between Carroll and Lafayette counties. Before the bridges, Joseph O. Shelby operated steamboats, a hemp plantation, ropeworks and a sawmill here. He also helped lead the Blue Lodge, an organization dedicated to making Kansas a slave state, before joining the Confederate cause in 1861.
